Most of the world's electricity comes from a machine invented in 1884. Newcastle, 1884. Charles Parsons, an earl's son, had trained as an engineer, and rival turbines were limited by the forces on their spinning parts.

His idea was to split the steam's fall into many small steps. His first turbine turned 18,000 times a minute, made 7.5 kilowatts and was 1.6 per cent efficient. In 1894 he built a boat to prove it. The first trials, with one propeller, were disappointing, so he fitted three shafts and nine propellers. At Spithead in 1897 it reached 34 knots, against 27 for the Navy's fastest. In 1905 the Admiralty chose turbines for all future ships. Today, over 90 per cent of the world's electricity comes from steam turbines.
